title: Drafting Proposals from Past Work
answer: Drafting proposals from past work means reusing and adapting text, aims, budgets, and supporting materials from earlier grant applications to answer a new funding call. crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Drafting proposals from past work means reusing and adapting text, aims, budgets, and supporting materials from earlier grant applications to answer a new funding call. It covers the whole proposal, including the project summary, specific aims, background, methods, timeline, budget justification, biosketches, and data management plan. The practice is common in academic and nonprofit research offices, where a strong prior award is treated as a starting point rather than a finished document. The goal is to save time while keeping the new proposal accurate, specific to the new call, and honest about what is new and what is carried over.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on a document repository of past proposals, award notices, reviewer comments, and progress reports, usually held in a shared drive or grants management system. Reference managers, word processors, spreadsheet budgets, and funder portals are the everyday tools, with institutional templates and checklists layered on top. Some teams add retrieval and drafting assistants that search their own archive, and a library of 288 research papers and 13755 extracted claims can help locate evidence and prior language. Version control matters because multiple writers, grants officers, and principal investigators touch the same files before submission.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: A typical pass starts by reading the new call and mapping its review criteria to sections of a past proposal that already scored well. Writers pull forward the stable parts, such as facilities, equipment, and team roles, then rewrite the aims, significance, and methods to match the new science and the new sponsor's language. They check every claim against current data, update preliminary results, and remove text that no longer applies. A glossary of 686 terms can keep terminology consistent across sections, and a final read by someone outside the project catches gaps and stale references.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk center on self-plagiarism, copyright, confidentiality, and funder disclosure rules. Reusing text from a prior proposal can breach a sponsor's originality policy or a confidentiality agreement, even when the author wrote the original. Provenance matters, so teams keep a record of which sentences came from which past document and who edited them. Many funders now ask whether generative AI was used in drafting, and reviewers expect all cited work to point to the original paper rather than a search summary.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction is toward structured proposal libraries that store reusable modules, evidence links, and compliance metadata alongside the text. Retrieval systems will get better at matching a new call to past funded work and at flagging outdated numbers or unsupported claims. Funder policies on AI assistance and text reuse will keep changing, so teams will need lightweight audit trails as a normal part of proposal writing. The likely result is less blank-page drafting and more careful assembly, review, and tailoring of material that already exists.
